text:
We start with the following SDE

$$
dX(t)=-aX(t)dt+\sigma dW(t), \quad t\in [0,T],
$$

where $X(0)=x_0$, $a>$ is a constant mean reversion rate and $\sigma>0$ is a deterministic volatility. Note that such a process is a base process for the Hull-White model and for the energy pricing models. Since for $t>s$

$$
X(t)=e^{-a(t-s)}X(s)+e^{-at}\int\limits_s^t e^{au}\sigma dW(u),
$$

the random variables $X(s)$ and $\displaystyle{\int\limits_s^t e^{au}\sigma dW(u)}$ are independent, and

$$
\sigma^2e^{-2at}\int\limits_s^te^{2au}du=\frac{\sigma^2}{2a}\Bigl(1-e^{-2a(t-s)}\Bigr),
$$

we get that

$$
f_{X(t_{k+1})|X(t_{k})}(x|x_k)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{\sigma^2}{2a}\Bigl(1-e^{-2ah}\Bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2}}\exp\Biggl(-\frac{(x-e^{-ah}x_k)^2}{\frac{\sigma^2}{a}\Bigl(1-e^{-2ah}\Bigr)}\Biggr).
$$

The negative log-likelihood is as follows

$$
&&\mathcal{L}(a,\sigma)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl[\frac{1}{2}\ln\Bigl(2\pi\cdot \frac{\sigma^2}{2a}\Bigl(1-e^{-2ah}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\
&&\quad\quad\quad\quad+\frac{a}{\sigma^2(1-e^{-2ah})}(x_{k+1}-e^{-ah}x_k)^2\Bigr].
$$

We reparametrize it in terms of

$$
&&A=e^{-ah},\\
&&\Sigma=\frac{\sigma^2}{2a}\Bigl(1-e^{-2ah}\Bigr),
$$

and obtain

$$
\mathcal{L}(A,\Sigma)=\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi\Sigma)+\frac{1}{2\Sigma}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(x_{k+1}-Ax_k)^2.
$$

We have that

$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A}=\frac{1}{\Sigma}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(x_{k+1}-Ax_k)\cdot (-x_k),
$$

and

$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \Sigma}=\frac{n}{2\Sigma}-\frac{1}{2\Sigma^2}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(x_{k+1}-Ax_k)^2.
$$

From $\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial A}=0$ we have

$$
A=\frac{\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_kx_{k+1}}{\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_k^2},
$$

while from $\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \Sigma}=0$,

$$
\Sigma=\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(x_{k+1}-A x_k)^2.
$$

Using we arrive at the following ML estimators of $a$ and $\sigma^2$

$$
\widehat{a}_n=-\frac{1}{h}\ln\Biggl(\frac{\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_kx_{k+1}}{\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_k^2}\Biggr),
$$

$$
\widehat{\sigma^2_n}=\frac{1}{n}\cdot\Biggl(\frac{2\widehat{a}_n}{1-e^{-2\widehat{a}_n h}}\Biggr)\cdot\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl(x_{k+1}-e^{-2\widehat{a}_n h}x_k\Bigr)^2.
$$
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
We now deal with the following OU process

$$
dX(t)=\kappa(\mu-X(t))dt+\sigma dW(t), \quad t\in [0,T],
$$

which is also called the Vasicek process. For $t>s$ we have

$$
X(t)=e^{-\kappa (t-s)}X(s)+\mu(1-e^{-\kappa (t-s)})+\sigma e^{-\kappa t}\int\limits_s^t e^{\kappa u}dW(u),
$$

and hence

$$
f_{X(t_{k+1})|X(t_{k})}(x|x_k)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\Bigl(1-e^{-2\kappa h}\Bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2}}\exp\Biggl(-\frac{(x-\mu(1-e^{-\kappa h})-e^{-\kappa h}x_k)^2}{\frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa}\Bigl(1-e^{-2\kappa h}\Bigr)}\Biggr).
$$

In this case the negative log-likelihood is as follows

$$
&&\mathcal{L}(\mu,\sigma,\kappa)=\frac{n}{2}\ln\Bigl(2\pi\cdot \frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\Bigl(1-e^{-2\kappa h}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\
&&\quad\quad\quad\quad+\frac{\kappa}{\sigma^2(1-e^{-2\kappa h})}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(x_{k+1}-\mu-e^{-\kappa h}(x_k-\mu))^2,
$$

and we reparametrise it in the following way

$$
&&A=e^{-\kappa h},\\
&&\Sigma=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}\Bigl(1-e^{-2\kappa h}\Bigr).
$$

This gives

$$
\mathcal{L}(\mu,\Sigma,A)=\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi \Sigma)+\frac{1}{2\Sigma}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(x_{k+1}-\mu-e^{-\kappa h}(x_k-\mu))^2.
$$

Minimalization of $\mathcal{L}$ gives the following ML estimators $$
&&\widehat{\kappa}_n=-h^{-1}\ln(\widehat{\beta}_{1,n}),\\

&&\widehat{\mu}_n=\widehat{\beta}_{2,n},\\

&&\widehat{\sigma^2}_n=2\widehat{\kappa}_n\widehat{\beta}_{3,n}(1-\widehat{\beta}^2_{n,1})^{-1},

$$ where $$

\widehat{\beta}_{1,n}=\frac{n^{-1}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_{k+1}x_k-n^{-2}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_{k+1}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_{k}}{n^{-1}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x^2_{k}-n^{-2}\Bigl(\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}x_{k}\Bigr)^2},

$$ $$

\widehat{\beta}_{2,n}=\frac{n^{-1}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}(x_{k+1}-\widehat{\beta}_{1,n}x_k)}{1-\widehat{\beta}_{1,n}},

$$ and $$

\widehat{\beta}_{3,n}=n^{-1}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl(x_{k+1}-\widehat{\beta}_{1,n}x_k-\widehat{\beta}_{2,n}(1-\widehat{\beta}_{1,n})\Bigr)^2,
$$ see .
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
Finally, we investigate the following OU-type process

$$
dX(t)=\kappa X(t)(\mu-\ln(X(t)))dt+\sigma X(t) dW(t), \quad t\in [0,T],
$$

with $X(0)=x_0>0$, which is called geometric Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. It can be shown by the use of Itô formula that $0<X(t)=\exp(U(t))$ where

$$
dU(t)=\kappa (\bar \mu-U(t))dt+\sigma dW(t), \quad t\in [0,T],
$$

and $\bar\mu=\mu-\frac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}$. Having the discrete observations $x_0,\ldots,x_n$ of $X$ we take $u_k=\ln x_k$ as the observations of $U$. Now we can use - in order to obtain the estimators $\widehat{\kappa}_n, \widehat{\bar\mu}_n,\widehat{\sigma^2}_n$ that are based on the values $(u_k)_{k=0}^n$. The estimator of $\mu$ is defined by

$$
\widehat{\mu}_n=\widehat{\bar\mu}_n+\frac{\widehat{\sigma^2}_n}{2\widehat{\kappa}_n}.
$$
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
Let us consider the general problem of estimating unknown parameters of the following scalar SDE

$$
dX(t)=a(t,X(t),\theta)dt+b(t,X(t),\theta)dW(t), \quad t\in [0,T]
$$

where the solution $X$ is sampled at the discrete points $t_i=iT/n$, $i=0,1,\ldots,n$, and $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are the realisations of $X$ at $t_i$'s. We also assume that $X(0)=x_0$ and $b(t,x,\theta)>0$ for all $(t,x,\theta)\in [0,T]\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^s$. Morever, $a,b:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^s\to\mathbb{R}$ are (at least) Borel measurable, $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^s$ and we assume that X is the unique strong solution of . For such a case the explicit form of the transition density is not known. However, for the Euler scheme, defined as follows

$$
X^E(t_0)=x_0,
$$

$$
X^E(t_{k+1})=X^E(t_{k})+a(t_k,X^E(t_{k}),\theta)h+b(t_k,X^E(t_{k}),\theta)\Delta W_k, \quad k =0,1,\ldots,n-1,
$$

we have the following conditional law

$$
X^E(t_{k+1})|X^E(t_{k})\sim N(X^E(t_{k})+a(t_k,X^E(t_{k}),\theta)h, h|b(t_k,X^E(t_{k}),\theta)|^2).
$$

Hence, we approximate the transition density with the following

$$
f_{X^E(t_{k+1})|X^E(t_{k})}(x|x_k)=\frac{1}{(2\pi b^2(t_k,x_k,\theta))^{1/2}}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(x-x_k-a(t_k,x_k,\theta)h)^2}{2hb^2(t_k,x_k,\theta)}\Bigr).
$$

Hence, the negative log-quasi likelihood is defined by

$$
&&\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}\ln f_{X^E(t_{k+1})|X^E(t_{k})}(x_{k+1}|x_k)\\
&&=\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-1}\Bigl[\ln (2\pi h b^2(t_k,x_k,\theta))+\frac{(x_{k+1}-x_k-a(t_k,x_k,\theta)h)^2}{hb^2(t_k,x_k,\theta)}\Bigr].
$$

We obtain the quasi maximum likelihood estimator $\hat\theta_n$ of $\theta$ by minimizing $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ with respect to $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^s$, i.e.

$$
\hat\theta_n=argmin_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^s}\mathcal{L}(\theta).
$$

Mostly, such minimalisation has to be done numerically.

**Remark.** *The approach described in this section can be extended in order to cover the multidimensional case.*

**Remark.** *We considered the case when the unknown estimated parameters $\theta$ do not depend on time. However, in more realistic models such parameters are often time-dependent. In such a case parameter estimation is much more involved and differs a lot from the time-independent case. See, for example, where application of artificial neural network is discussed in the context of estimation of time-dependent $\theta$.*
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
Having calibrated SDE-based model on $[0,T]$ to the real data $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n$ we can make predictions for $t>T$. Namely, outside the interval $[0,T]$ we consider the following SDE

$$
d\hat X(t)=a(t,\hat X(t),\hat\theta_n)dt+b(t,\hat X(t),\hat\theta_n)dW(t), \quad t\in [T,T+\Delta],
$$

where $\hat X(T)=x_n$, $\Delta>0$ is the length of the prediction horizon, $W=[W^1,\ldots,W^m]^T$ is $m$-dimensional Wiener process, and $\hat\theta_n$ is the estimated value of the true parameter $\theta$. W also assume that $a(t,x,\theta)$, $b(t,x,\theta)$ are defined for all $(t,x,\theta)\in [T,T+\Delta]\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^s$. We now describe (inductively) the forecasting procedure together with the construction of prediction intervals at confidence level $\alpha\in (0,1)$ (which we take in practice close to $1$). Since in general we do not know the analytical solution $\hat X$, the prediction procedure is based on the Euler-Maruyama scheme that approximates $\hat X$. Note that there are many trajectories that we can obtain as predictions of future behavior of $\hat X$. We can handle with this problem by computing a (suitable) single trajectory together with prediction intervals (at confidence level $\alpha$) around it.

Let us take $h=\Delta/N$ for some $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $t_k=T+kh$ for $k=0,1,\ldots,N.$
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)
section: Monte Carlo forecasting in SDE-based models

text:
**Approach 1:** Assume that $\bar x_k$ is given prediction of the value of $\hat X(t_k)$ (for $k=0$ we have $\bar x_0:=x_n$). The one step of Euler-Maruyama scheme from $\bar x_k$ at the time $t_k$ to $t_{k+1}=t_k+h$ is defined as follows

$$
\bar X^E_N(t_{k+1})=\bar x_k+a(t_k,\bar x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot h+b(t_k,\bar x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot \Delta W_k,
$$

where $\Delta W_k=W(t_{k+1})-W(t_k)$. As in the Section , let $q_{\alpha}$ be the two-sided $\alpha$-quantile of the normal distribution $N(0,1)$. We define the prediction interval for (the unknown value) $\hat X(t_{k+1})$ as follows

$$
\mathcal{\bar P}_{k+1}(\alpha):=\Bigl[\bar\mu_{k+1}-q_{\alpha}\cdot\bar\sigma_{k+1},\bar\mu_{k+1}+q_{\alpha}\cdot\bar\sigma_{k+1}\Bigr],
$$

with

$$
&&\bar\mu_{k+1}:=\bar x_k+a(t_k,\bar x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot h,\\
&&\bar\sigma_{k+1}:=\sqrt{h}\cdot |b(t_k,\bar x_k,\hat\theta_n)|.
$$

If $b(t_k,\bar x_k,\hat\theta_n)\neq 0$ then we have

$$
\mathbb{P}(\bar X^E_N(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\bar P}_{k+1}(\alpha))=\mathbb{P}(|\bar X^E_N(t_{k+1})-\bar\mu_{k+1}|\leq q_{\alpha}\cdot\bar\sigma_{k+1})=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\frac{|\Delta W_k|}{\sqrt{h}}\leq q_{\alpha}\Bigr)=\alpha,
$$

while if $b(t_k,\bar x_k,\hat\theta_n)=0$ then $\bar X^E_N(t_{k+1})=\bar\mu_{k+1}$ with probability one. Since $\bar X^E_N(t_{k+1})\approx \hat X(t_{k+1})$ and the law of $\bar X^E_N(t_{k+1})$ is $N(\bar\mu_{k+1},\bar\sigma^2_{k+1})$ (if $\bar\sigma_{k+1}>0$), in the case when $\bar\sigma_{k+1}>0$ the prediction $\bar x_{k+1}$ of the value $\hat X(t_{k+1})$ we take as a number drawn from the distribution $N(\bar\mu_{k+1},\bar\sigma^2_{k+1})$, while $\bar x_{k+1}:=\bar x_k+a(t_k,\bar x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot h$ if $\bar\sigma_{k+1}=0$.

The drawback of this approach is that, with a small probability $1-\alpha$ but still, the drawn value $\bar x_{k+1}$ may lie outside the prediction interval $\mathcal{\bar P}_{k+1}(\alpha)$. We overcome this problem in the Approach 2.\
\
**Approach 2:** Assume that we have given $\bar x_k$ and $\tilde x_k$, where $\bar x_k$ is the prediction of the value of $\hat X(t_k)$ and $\tilde x_k$ is equal to $\tilde X^E_N(t_k)$- the simulated value of Euler-Maruyama scheme at $t_k$ (for $k=0$ we take $\tilde x_0=\bar x_0:=x_n$). The one step of Euler-Maruyama scheme from $t_k$ to $t_{k+1}=t_k+h$, starting from $\tilde x_k$ at $t_k$, is defined as follows
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)
section: Prediction intervals in the scalar case with $m=d=1$

text:
$$
\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})=\tilde x_k+a(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot h+b(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot \Delta W_k,
$$

where $\Delta W_k=W(t_{k+1})-W(t_k)$ is the increment of the Wiener process that is independent of $\Sigma_{t_k}$ and, therefore, also of $\tilde X^E_N(t_k)$. Again, let $q_{\alpha}$ be the two-sided $\alpha$-quantile of the normal distribution $N(0,1)$. We define the prediction interval for (the unknown value) $\hat X(t_{k+1})$ as follows

$$
\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha):=\Bigl[\tilde\mu_{k+1}-q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_{k+1},\tilde\mu_{k+1}+q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_{k+1}\Bigr],
$$

with

$$
&&\tilde\mu_{k+1}:=\tilde x_k+a(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot h,\\
&&\tilde\sigma_{k+1}:=\sqrt{h}\cdot |b(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)|.
$$

Note that it holds $\tilde\mu_{k+1}=\mathbb{E}(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1}) \ | \ \Sigma_{t_k})$ and $\tilde\sigma^2_{k+1}=Var(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1}) \ | \ \Sigma_{t_k})$. If $b(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\neq 0$, then we have

$$
&&\mathbb{P}(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha) \ | \ \Sigma_{t_k})=\mathbb{P}(|\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})-\tilde\mu_{k+1}|\leq q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_{k+1}\ | \ \Sigma_{t_k})\\
&&=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\frac{|\Delta W_k|}{\sqrt{h}}\leq q_{\alpha}\ | \ \Sigma_{t_k}\Bigr)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\frac{|\Delta W_k|}{\sqrt{h}}\leq q_{\alpha}\Bigr)=\alpha,
$$

and hence

$$
\mathbb{P}(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha) )=\alpha,
$$

while if $b(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)=0$, then $\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})=\tilde\mu_{k+1}$ with probability one. Now, the main difference, when comparing to the Approach 1, is that in the Approach 2 we take

$$
\bar x_{k+1}:=\tilde \mu_{k+1}
$$

as the predicted value of $\hat X(t_{k+1})$, while for the next starting point for the one step of the Euler-Maruyama scheme we set

$$
\tilde x_{k+1}:= \tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})
$$

if $\tilde\sigma^2_{k+1}>0$, and $\tilde x_{k+1}:=\tilde\mu_{k+1}$ if $\tilde\sigma_{k+1}=0$. (Hence, for fixed $\tilde x_k$, the value of $\tilde x_{k+1}$ might be drawn from the distribution $N(\tilde\mu_{k+1},\tilde\sigma^2_{k+1})$.) In this approach the predicted value $\bar x_{k+1}$ is the mid point of $\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha)$, while the drawn next starting point $\tilde x_{k+1}$ may lie outside the prediction interval $\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha)$ but with (small) probability $1-\alpha$.
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)
section: Prediction intervals in the scalar case with $m=d=1$

text:
The procedure described in Approach 2 of Monte Carlo forecasting for SDEs might be implemented as follows:

- draw independent random samples $Z_0,Z_1,\ldots,Z_{N-1}$ form the distribution $N(0,1)$,

- let $\tilde x_0:=x_n$ and for $k=0,1,\ldots,N-1$ compute

$$
\tilde x_{k+1}=\tilde x_{k}+a(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot h+ \sqrt{h}\cdot b(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot Z_k,
$$

- having $\{\tilde x_k\}_{k=0,1,\ldots,N}$, take $\bar x_0:=x_n$ and compute for $k=1,2,\ldots, N$ the predictions $\bar x_k$ and the prediction intervals $\mathcal{\tilde P}_k(\alpha)$ as follows

$$
&&\bar x_k = \tilde\mu_k=\tilde x_{k-1}+a(t_{k-1},\tilde x_{k-1},\hat\theta_n)\cdot h,\\
&&\tilde\sigma_k=\sqrt{h}\cdot |b(t_{k-1},\tilde x_{k-1},\hat\theta_n)|,\\
&&\mathcal{\tilde P}_k(\alpha)=[\tilde\mu_k-q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_k, \tilde\mu_k+q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_k].
$$

**Remark.** *In the case when we have access to the real data (ground truth) at the time $t_k$ we can take it as the staring point $\tilde x_k$ for the one step of the Euler-Maruyama algorithm (from $t_k$ to $t_{k+1}$) in the Approach 2.*

**Remark.** *Note that if we take $\tilde x_k=\bar x_k=\tilde\mu_k$ for all $k$ (no matter if $\tilde\sigma^2_k=0$ or not) in the Approach 2, then $(\tilde x_k)_{k=0,1,\ldots,N}$ corresponds the the Euler scheme when applied to the following ODE

$$
\hat x'(t)=a(t,\hat x(t),\hat\theta_n), \quad t\in [T,T+\Delta], \quad \hat x(T)=x_n.
$$

The drawback is that we lose in this case information about the noise modeled in - the prediction of $\hat X$ is oversmoothed.*

We define the following functions

$$
&&\tilde\mu_{k+1}(x)=x+h\cdot a(t_k,x,\hat\theta_n),\\
&&\tilde\sigma^2_{k+1}(x)=h\cdot b^2(t_k,x,\hat\theta_n),
$$

and let

$$
\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha,x)=[\tilde\mu_{k+1}(x)-q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_{k+1}(x),\tilde\mu_{k+1}(x)+q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_{k+1}(x)].
$$

Then, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N-1$

$$
A_{k+1}:=\{\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha,\tilde X^E_N(t_{k}))\}=\{|\Delta W_k|\leq q_{\alpha}\cdot\sqrt{h}\},
$$

and hence, the sets $(A_k)_{k=1,\ldots,N}$ are independent. This implies that

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcap_{k=0}^{N-1}A_{k+1}\Bigr)=\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{P}(A_{k+1})=\alpha^N,
$$

which gives the probability for the *simultaneous prediction interval*

$$
\bigtimes_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(\alpha,\tilde X^E_N(t_{k})).
$$
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)
section: Prediction intervals in the scalar case with $m=d=1$

text:
Let us take, as in the one-dimensional case, that

$$
\tilde\mu_{k+1}(x):= x+h\cdot a(t_k,x,\hat\theta_n), \quad x\in\mathbb{R}^d.
$$

Assume that we have given $\bar x_k$ and $\tilde x_k$, where $\bar x_k$ is the prediction of the value of $\hat X(t_k)$ and $\tilde x_k$ is equal to $\tilde X^E_N(t_k)$- the simulated value of Euler-Maruyama scheme at $t_k$ (for $k=0$ we take $\tilde x_0=\bar x_0:=x_n$). Then for the one step of Euler-Maruyama scheme from $t_k$ to $t_{k+1}=t_k+h$, starting from $\tilde x_k$ at $t_k$, we have

$$
b^T(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot\Bigl(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(\tilde x_k)\Bigr)=(b^Tb)(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot\Delta W_k=\sqrt{h}\cdot (b^Tb)(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot Z_k,
$$

where $Z_k:=\Delta W_k/\sqrt{h}$ has $m$-dimensional normal distribution $N(0,I_m)$. We impose the following assumption

$$
(M) \ \ \hbox{for all} \ (t,x,z) \ \hbox{the matrix} \ b(t,x,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} \ \hbox{has} \ m \ \hbox{linearly independent columns, i.e.} \ rank(b(t,x,z))=m.
$$

Since for all $(t,x,z)$ we have $rank(b(t,x,z))\leq\min\{d,m\}$, the assumption (M) implies that

$$
d\geq m.
$$

Then, for all $(t,x,z)$, the matrix $(b^Tb)(t,x,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ is symmetric and positive definite. Hence,

$$
h^{-1/2}\cdot (b^Tb)^{-1}(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot b^T(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot\Bigl(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(\tilde x_k)\Bigr)=Z_k=\Delta W_k/\sqrt{h}
$$

has normal distribution $N(0,I_m)$. Therefore, for $B(0,R)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m \ | \ \|x\|\leq R\}$, $R\in [0,+\infty]$, we have

$$
&&p(R)=\mathbb{P}\Biggl( h^{-1/2}\cdot (b^Tb)^{-1}(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot b^T(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot\Bigl(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(\tilde x_k)\Bigr)\in B(0,R)\Biggr)\\
&&=\int\limits_{B(0,R)}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{m/2}}e^{-\|x\|^2/2}dx,
$$

and we call $p(R)$ the *confidence level*. For all $y\in\mathbb{R}^d$ we define

$$
\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,y)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d \ | \ h^{-1/2}\|b^+(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n)\cdot (z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))\|\leq R\},
$$

where

$$
b^+(t,y,z):=(b^Tb)^{-1}(t,y,z)\cdot b^T(t,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}
$$

is the Moore-Penrose inverse of $b(t,y,z)$, since we have assumed that $rank(b(t,y,z))=m$ and $d\geq m$, see . Note that $b^+(t,y,z)$ is also the left-inverse of $b(t,y,z)$, since

$$
b^+(t,y,z)\cdot b(t,y,z)=I_m.
$$

Moreover, if we denote by
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)
section: Ellipsoidal prediction regions in multidimensional case

text:
$$
E_k(y):=(b^+(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n))^T\cdot b^+(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n),
$$

then we can write

$$
\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,y)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d \ | \ (z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))^T\cdot E_k(y)\cdot (z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))\leq h R^2\}.
$$

For all $y\in\mathbb{R}^d$ the matrix $E_k(y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ is symmetric and positive semi-definite, and for all $y,z\in\mathbb{R}^d$

$$
(z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))^T\cdot E_k(y)\cdot (z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))=\|b^+(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n)\cdot (z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))\|^2\geq 0.
$$

We define the *prediction region* for $\hat X(t_{k+1})$ as

$$
\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(R):=\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,\tilde x_k).
$$

Then

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(R) \ | \ \Sigma_{t_k}\Bigr)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(h^{-1/2}\|\Delta W_k\|\leq R \ | \ \Sigma_{t_k}\Bigr)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(h^{-1/2}\|\Delta W_k\|\leq R \Bigr)=p(R),
$$

and therefore

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(R) \Bigr)=p(R).
$$

We take

$$
\bar x_{k+1}:=\tilde \mu_{k+1}(\tilde x_k)=\tilde x_k+h\cdot a(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)
$$

as the predicted value of $\hat X(t_{k+1})$, while for the next starting point for the one step of the Euler-Maruyama scheme we set

$$
\tilde x_{k+1}:= \tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1}).
$$

Hence, for fixed $\tilde x_k$, the value of $\tilde x_{k+1}$ might be drawn from the distribution $N(\tilde\mu_{k+1}(\tilde x_k),\tilde V^2_{k+1}(\tilde x_k))$, where $\tilde V^2_{k+1}(y):=h\cdot (bb^T)(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n)$.

The procedure of Monte Carlo forecasting for SDEs might be described as follows:

- draw independent random samples $Z_0,Z_1,\ldots,Z_{N-1}$ form the distribution $N(0,I_m)$,

- let $\tilde x_0:=x_n$ and for $k=0,1,\ldots,N-1$ compute

$$
\tilde x_{k+1}=\tilde x_{k}+a(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot h+ \sqrt{h}\cdot b(t_k,\tilde x_k,\hat\theta_n)\cdot Z_k,
$$

- having $\{\tilde x_k\}_{k=0,1,\ldots,N}$, take $\bar x_0:=x_n$, then, for $k=1,2,\ldots, N$, compute the predictions $\bar x_k$ and set the prediction regions $\mathcal{\tilde P}_k(R)$ as follows

$$
&&\bar x_k = \tilde\mu_k=\tilde x_{k-1}+a(t_{k-1},\tilde x_{k-1},\hat\theta_n)\cdot h,\\
%&&\tilde\sigma_k=\sqrt{h}\cdot |b(t_{k-1},\tilde x_{k-1},\hat\theta_n)|,\\
&&\mathcal{\tilde P}_k(R)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d \ | \ h^{-1/2}\|b^+(t_{k-1},\tilde x_{k-1},\hat\theta_n)\cdot (z-\tilde\mu_{k})\|\leq R\}.
$$

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N-1$

$$
A_{k+1}:=\{\tilde X^E_N(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,\tilde X^E_N(t_{k}))\}=\{\|\Delta W_k\|\leq R\cdot\sqrt{h}\}=\{Z_k\in B(0,R)\},
$$

and hence, the sets $(A_k)_{k=1,\ldots,N}$ are independent. This implies that

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl((\tilde X^E_N(t_1),\tilde X^E_N(t_2),\ldots, \tilde X^E_N(t_N))\in \bigtimes_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,\tilde X^E_N(t_{k}))\Bigr)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcap_{k=0}^{N-1}A_{k+1}\Bigr)=\prod_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathbb{P}(A_{k+1})=(p(R))^N,
$$

which gives the probability that the obtained $N$-step prediction $(\tilde X^E_N(t_1),\tilde X^E_N(t_2),\ldots, \tilde X^E_N(t_N))$ belongs to the *simultaneous prediction region*

$$
\bigtimes_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,\tilde X^E_N(t_{k})).
$$

In a special case we can describe the geometry of $\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,y)$ in a more precise way. Namely, let us assume that for all $(t,y,z)$

$$
rank(b^+(t,y,z))=d.
$$

Since $rank(b^+(t,y,z))=d\leq \min\{d,m\}\leq m$, by this assumption force the following

$$
d=m,
$$

and the matrix $b(t,y,z)$ has to be a square matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$. Moreover, it is of full rank (equal to $d$), and therefore it is also non-singular. In this case for all $(t,y,z)$

$$
b^+(t,y,z)=b^{-1}(t,y,z),
$$

and the symmetric matrix

$$
E_k(y)=\Bigl(b(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n)\cdot b^T(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n)\Bigr)^{-1}
$$

is positive definite (In particular, this also implies that $\tilde V^2_{k+1}(y)$ is positive definite, since $\tilde V^2_{k+1}(y)=h\cdot E^{-1}_{k}(y)$.) Moreover,

$$
&&\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,y)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d \ | \ h^{-1/2}\|b^{-1}(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n)\cdot (z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))\|\leq R\}\\
&&=\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y)+h^{1/2}b(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n) B(0,R),
$$

and, therefore, in the case when $E_k(y)$ is positive definite, the set $\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,y)$ is an ellipsoid centered at $\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y)$. The eigenvectors of $E_k(y)/(hR^2)$ are the principal axes of the ellipsoid, and length of each corresponding semi-axe is $1/(\lambda_j(y))^{1/2}$, where $\lambda_j(y)$'s are the (strictly positive) eigenvalues of $E_k(y)/(hR^2)$.

**Remark.** *Note that we can write $\tilde V^2_{k+1}(y)=(\tilde V_{k+1}(y))^T\cdot \tilde V_{k+1}(y)$ where

$$
\tilde V_{k+1}(y)=h^{1/2}\cdot b^T(t_k,y,\hat\theta_n),
$$

and

$$
\mathcal{P}_{k+1}(R,y)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d \ | \ \|[\tilde V_{k+1}(y) \tilde V^T_{k+1}(y)]^{-1}\tilde V_{k+1}(y)(z-\tilde\mu_{k+1}(y))\|\leq R\}
$$

The procedure described in the previous section of obtaining prediction regions in multidimensional case takes into account the fact that coordinates of $\hat X$ and $\tilde X^E_N$ are correlated. Because of that it is possible to compute explicitly:

- the probability that all of the coordinates $\tilde X^E_{N,j}$ are in $\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1}(R)$ simultaneously,

- the probability that the whole predicted $N$-steps forward belong to the simultaneous prediction region .

One can however try an alternative (and, at first sight, more natural) approach in which one computes prediction intervals for each coordinate $\hat X_j$ separately (by using an approach known from the one-dimensional case) and then takes a Cartesian product of them (which is in fact a hypercube in $\mathbb{R}^d$). However, there is a pitfall in that approach, which we now describe in detail.

Note that for all $j=1,2,\ldots,d$, $k=0,1,\ldots,N-1$

$$
\tilde X^E_{N,j}(t_{k+1})\ | \ \Sigma_{t_k}\sim N\Bigl(\tilde\mu_{k+1,j}(\tilde X^E_{N}(t_{k})), \tilde\sigma^2_{k+1,j}(\tilde X^E_{N}(t_{k}))\Bigr),
$$

where for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$

$$
&&\tilde\mu_{k+1,j}(x)=x_j+h \cdot a_j(t_k,x,\hat\theta_n),\\
&&\tilde\sigma^2_{k+1,j}(x)=h\cdot\sum_{l=1}^m (b(t_k,x,\hat\theta_n))^2.
$$

Let us take

$$
\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1,j}(\alpha,x)=[\tilde\mu_{k+1,j}(x)-q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_{k+1,j}(x), \tilde\mu_{k+1,j}(x)+q_{\alpha}\cdot\tilde\sigma_{k+1,j}(x)],
$$

and

$$
B_{k+1,j}=\{\tilde X^E_{N,j}(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1,j}(\alpha,\tilde X^E_{N}(t_{k}))\},
$$

then, by , we have for all $j=1,2,\ldots,d$ that

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(B_{k+1,j} \ | \ \Sigma_{t_k}\Bigr)=\mathbb{P}\Biggl(\frac{|\tilde X^E_{N,j}(t_{k+1})-\tilde\mu_{k+1,j}(\tilde X^E_{N}(t_{k}))|}{\tilde\sigma_{k+1,j}(\tilde X^E_{N}(t_{k}))}\leq q_{\alpha} \ \Bigl| \ \Sigma_{t_k}\Biggr)=\alpha,
$$

and hence for each coordinate of $\tilde X^E_{N}(t_{k+1})$ we have

$$
\mathbb{P}(B_{k+1,j})=\alpha.
$$

Note that for fixed $k=1,2,\ldots,d$ the sets

$$B_{k+1,1},B_{k+1,2},\ldots, B_{k+1,d}$$

are not independent (even conditionally wrt $\Sigma_{t_k}$). Therefore, we do not have the exact value (or at least good estimates) of the probability

$$
\mathbb{P}(B_{k+1})=\mathbb{P}(\tilde X^E_{N}(t_{k+1})\in\mathcal{\tilde B}_{k+1}(\alpha,\tilde X^E_N(t_k))),
$$

where

$$
B_{k+1}=\bigcap_{j=1}^d B_{k+1,j}
$$

and

$$
\mathcal{\tilde B}_{k+1}(\alpha,x)=\bigtimes_{j=1}^d\mathcal{\tilde P}_{k+1,j}(\alpha,x).
$$

Moreover, the sets $\{B_{k+1}\}_{k=0,1,\ldots,N-1}$ are also not independent. Hence, in general it is not known how to compute the probability

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl((\tilde X^E_N(t_1),\tilde X^E_N(t_2),\ldots,\tilde X^E_N(t_N))\in\bigtimes_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathcal{\tilde B}_{k+1}(\alpha,\tilde X^E_N(t_k))\Bigr)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcap_{k=0}^{N-1}B_{k+1}\Bigr),
$$

and this method of constructing prediction regions do not allows us to control the probability that the whole predicted sequence belong to the simultaneous prediction region. This is an obvious drawback.

In this notes we use many results from the theory of stochastic processes, including basics from measure and probability theory. We will now recall some of them. For a comprehensive exposition see, for example, , , , , , , , , .

By $\|\cdot\|_2$ we mean the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^d$.

Let $X$ be an arbitrary set. A collection $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of $X$ is a *$\sigma$-field* on $X$ if

- $X\in\mathcal{A}$,

- for every $A\in\mathcal{A}$, the set $X\setminus A$ belongs to $\mathcal{A}$,

- for any infinite sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{A}$ we have that $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_n\in\mathcal{A}$,

- for any infinite sequence $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{A}$ we have that $\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_n\in\mathcal{A}$.

As we can see a $\sigma$-field on $X$ is a subclass of $2^X$[^2] that contains $X$ and is closed with respect to complementation, countable unions and intersections. Note also that, in the definition of $\sigma$-field we could have used only conditions $(i)$, $(ii)$, and $(iii)$, or only conditions $(i)$, $(ii)$, and $(iv)$, as it is sometimes in literature. Moreover, sometimes the authors use the term $\sigma$-algebra instead of $\sigma$-field.\
A measurable space is a pair $(X,\mathcal{A})$ where $X$ is a set and $\mathcal{A}$ is a $\sigma$-field on $X$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal{C}$ be an arbitrary class of subsets of $X$. By $\sigma(\mathcal{C})$ we denote the intersection of all those $\sigma$-fields that contain $\mathcal{C}$. It turns out that $\sigma(\mathcal{C})$ is the smallest $\sigma$-field that contains $\mathcal{C}$, and it is called the $\sigma$-field *generated* by $\mathcal{C}$. Such $\sigma$-field always exists, see, for example, Corollary in . If $\mathcal{C}$ is already a $\sigma$-field then $\sigma(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}$. Furthermore, the following holds (see, for example, ).

**Proposition.** *Let $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ be two families of subsets of $X$. Then:*

- *If $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{D}$ then $\sigma(\mathcal{C})\subset\sigma(\mathcal{D})$*

- *If $\mathcal{C}\subset\sigma(\mathcal{D})$ then $\sigma(\mathcal{C})\subset\sigma(\mathcal{D})$*

- *If $\mathcal{C}\subset\sigma(\mathcal{D})$ and $\mathcal{D}\subset\sigma(\mathcal{C})$, then $\sigma(\mathcal{C})=\sigma(\mathcal{D})$*

- *If $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{D}\subset\sigma(\mathcal{C})$, $\sigma(\mathcal{C})=\sigma(\mathcal{D})$*
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
- *If $\mathcal{C}\subset\sigma(\mathcal{D})$ and $\mathcal{D}\subset\sigma(\mathcal{C})$, then $\sigma(\mathcal{C})=\sigma(\mathcal{D})$*

- *If $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathcal{D}\subset\sigma(\mathcal{C})$, $\sigma(\mathcal{C})=\sigma(\mathcal{D})$*

The intersection of an arbitrary (even uncountable) class of $\sigma$-fields on $X$ is again a $\sigma$-field on $X$. This is not however true when considering union of $\sigma$-fields. Namely, except in some particular cases, the union of two $\sigma$-fields $\mathcal{A}_1$, $\mathcal{A}_2$ on $X$ is not a $\sigma$-field. The $\sigma$-field generated by $\mathcal{A}_1\cup\mathcal{A}_2$ is denoted by $\mathcal{A}_1\vee \mathcal{A}_2$,

$$
\mathcal{A}_1\vee \mathcal{A}_2:=\sigma(\mathcal{A}_1\cup\mathcal{A}_2).
$$

In general, if $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family of $\sigma$-fields on $X$, where the index set $I$ might be even uncountable, then we define

$$
\mathcal{A}_{I}:=\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i\Bigr),
$$

the $\sigma$-field generated by $\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i$. It is sometimes also denoted by $\bigvee_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i$. Note that the above definition of $\bigvee_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i$ is valid for a family $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ of arbitrary classes of subsets of $X$ (i.e., some of $\mathcal{A}_i$'s do not have to be $\sigma$-fields on $X$). This follows from the following fact.

**Proposition.** *Let $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of classes of subsets of $X$. Then

$$
\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i\Bigr)=\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\sigma(\mathcal{A}_i)\Bigr).
$$

*

**Proof.** Since for all $i\in I$ we have $\mathcal{A}_i\subset\sigma(\mathcal{A}_i)$, we obtain that $\displaystyle{\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i\subset\bigcup_{i\in I}\sigma(\mathcal{A}_i)}$ and hence

$$
\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i\Bigr)\subset\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\sigma(\mathcal{A}_i)\Bigr).
$$

On the other hand, $\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}_j\subset\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i}$ for all $j\in I$ and therefore $\displaystyle{\sigma(\mathcal{A}_j)\subset\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i\Bigr)}$ for all $j\in I$. Hence, $\displaystyle{\bigcup_{i\in I}\sigma(\mathcal{A}_i)\subset\sigma \Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i\Bigr)}$ and

$$
\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\sigma(\mathcal{A}_i)\Bigr)\subset \sigma \Bigl(\bigcup_{i\in I}\mathcal{A}_i\Bigr).
$$

If $X$ is a topological space, then the $\sigma$-field generated by the collection $Top X$ of all open subsets of $X$ is called the *Borel $\sigma$-field* on $X$ and it is denoted by $\mathcal{B}(X)$ (i.e., $\mathcal{B}(X)=\sigma(Top X)$). Its elements are called *Borel sets*.

Let $(X_1,\mathcal{A}_1)$ and $(X_2,\mathcal{A}_2)$ be two measurable spaces. A function $f:X_1\to X_2$ is called $\mathcal{A}_1$-to-$\mathcal{A}_2$ measurable (or $\mathcal{A}_1 / \mathcal{A}_2$-measurable) if

$$
f^{-1}(B)\in \mathcal{A}_1 \ \hbox{for all} \ B\in\mathcal{A}_2,
$$

where $\displaystyle{f^{-1}(B)=\{x\in X_1 \ | \ f(x)\in B}\}$. If $A\in\mathcal{A}_1$ then a function $f:A\to X_2$ is $\mathcal{A}_1 / \mathcal{A}_2$-measurable if $f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{A}_1$ for any $B\in\mathcal{A}_2$. Moreover, we define

$$
\sigma(f)=\{f^{-1}(B) \ | \ B\in\mathcal{A}_2\}.
$$

It turns out that $\sigma(f)$ is a $\sigma$-field on $X_1$ and it is the smallest $\sigma$-field on $X_1$ such that $f$ is measurable relative to it and $\mathcal{A}_2$ (i.e., $\sigma(f) / \mathcal{A}_2$-measurable). We call $\sigma(f)$ the $\sigma$-field generated by $f$. It is easy to check that $f$ is $\mathcal{A}_1 / \mathcal{A}_2$-measurable iff $\sigma(f)\subset\mathcal{A}_1$. Moreover, if $(X_3,\mathcal{A}_3)$ is a measurable space then for any two functions $f_1:X_1\to X_2$ and $f_2:X_2\to X_3$, where $f_2$ is $\mathcal{A}_2 / \mathcal{A}_3$-measurable, we have $\sigma(f_2\circ f_1)\subset\sigma(f_1)$. This implies the following fact.

**Proposition.** *Let $(X_i,\mathcal{A}_i)$, $i=1,2,3$, be measurable spaces, let $f_1:X_1\to X_2$ be $\mathcal{A}_1 /\mathcal{A}_2$-measurable, while $f_2:X_2\to X_3$ is assumed to be $\mathcal{A}_2/\mathcal{A}_3$-measurable. The the composition

$$
f_2\circ f_1:X_1\to X_3
$$

is $\mathcal{A}_1 / \mathcal{A}_3$-measurable.*

**Proposition.** *Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space, and let $A\subset X$. Then the function

$$
X\ni x \to \mathbf{1}_A(x)\in\{0,1\}
$$

is $\mathcal{A} / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable iff $A\in\mathcal{A}$.*

In the case when $X_2$ is topological space, equipped with the Borel $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{A}_2=\mathcal{B}(Top X_2)$, we refer to $\mathcal{A}_1 / \mathcal{B}(X_2)$-measurable function $f:X_1\to X_2$ as *Borel function*.

Below we give important examples of Borel functions.

**Proposition.**

text:
- *If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are topological spaces, and if $f:X_1\to X_2$ is continuous function then it is Borel measurable, that is $\mathcal{B}(X_1) / \mathcal{B}(X_2)$-measurable.*

- *Every right (left)-continuous function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is Borel. Hence, every càdlàg (càglàd) function is Borel measurable.*

- *If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ is a bounded variation function then $f$ is Borel measurable.*

- *Let $I$ be a subinterval of $\mathbb{R}$, and let $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be a monotone function. Then $f$ is Borel measurable.*

- *If $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is a convex function then it is continuous and hence, Borel measurable.*

Let us now assume that $(X_2,\|\cdot\|)$ is a real or complex Banach space and let $\mathcal{A}_2=\mathcal{B}(X_2)=\sigma(Top X_2)$. Then we have another notion of measurability. A function $f:X_1\to X_2$ is *strongly measurable* (or *Bochner measurable*) if it is Borel measurable and has separable range (i.e., $f(X_1)\subset X_2$ is separable). If $X_2$ is separable, then every $X_2$-valued Borel measurable function is strongly measurable. (It follows from the fact that a subset of separable metric space is itself separable.) Moreover, if $f:X_1\to X_2$ is Borel measurable, then

$$
X_1 \ni x\to \|f(x)\|\in [0,+\infty)
$$

is $\mathcal{A}_1 / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable. Moreover, we have the following important result, see .

**Theorem.** *Let $(X_1,\mathcal{A}_1)$ be a measurable space, and let $X_2$ be a real or complex Banach space. Then the set of all strongly measurable functions from $X_1$ to $X_2$ is a vector space.*

We want to stress here that the set of all Borel measurable functions from $X_1$ to $X_2$ can fail to be a vector space, see page 403 in . Therefore, separability of the range in the definition of strongly measurable function is crucial.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p\in [1,+\infty)$. Then we define

$$
L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu;\mathbb{R}^d)=\Bigl\{f:X\to\mathbb{R}^d \ \Bigl| \ f-\hbox{Borel function,} \int\limits_X \|f(x)\|_2^p\ \mu(dx)<+\infty \Bigr\}.
$$

If we identify functions which are equal $\mu$-almost everywhere, then $L^p(X,\mathcal{A},\mu;\mathbb{R}^d)$ is a Banach space with norm

$$
\|f\|_{L^p(X;\mathbb{R}^d)}=\Bigl(\int\limits_X \|f(x)\|_2^p\ \mu(dx)\Bigr)^{1/p}.
$$

For the case $d=1$ we simply write $L^p(X)$.

The proof of the following result can be found in .

**Theorem.** *(Change of measure in Lebesgue integral) Let $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$ be a measure space, let $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be a measurable space, and let $f:(X,\mathcal{A})\to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable. Let $g$ be an extended real-valued $\mathcal{B}$-measurable function on $Y$. Then $g$ is $\mu f^{-1}$-integrable if and only if $g\circ f$ is $\mu$-integrable. If these functions are integrable, then

$$
\int\limits_Y g d(\mu f^{-1})=\int\limits_X (g\circ f) d\mu.
$$

*

For the proof of the mean value theorem we refer to, for example, page 167 in .

**Theorem.** *(Mean value theorem) Let $E\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a connected set with $\lambda_d(E)<+\infty$. If $f:E\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous and bounded, then there exists $c\in E$ such that

$$
\int\limits_E f(x)\ \lambda_d(dx)=f(c)\cdot \lambda_d(E).
$$

*

We also recall fundamental integral inequalities, see, for example, .

**Theorem.** *(Hölder and Minkowski inequalities) For any Borel measurable real-valued functions $f$ and $g$ on some measure space $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$, we have*

- *for all $p,q,r>0$ with $p^{-1}+q^{-1}=r^{-1}$ that it holds

$$
\Bigl(\int\limits_X |f(x)g(x)|^r\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{1/r}\leq \Bigl(\int\limits_X |f(x)|^p\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{1/p}\cdot\Bigl(\int\limits_X |g(x)|^q\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{1/q},
$$

*

- *for all $p>0$

$$
\Bigl(\int\limits_X|f(x)+g(x)|^p\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{\min\{p,1\}/p}\leq\Bigl(\int\limits_X|f(x)|^p\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{\min\{p,1\}/p}+\Bigl(\int\limits_X|g(x)|^p\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{\min\{p,1\}/p}.
$$

*

**Theorem.** *(Jensen's inequality) For any random vector $\xi:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^d$, defined on a probability space $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$, and convex function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$, we have that

$$
f(\mathbb{E}\xi)\leq \mathbb{E}(f(\xi)).
$$

*

We also recall the very useful Gronwall's lemma for Lebesgue integrals, see, for example, or Annex C in , where more general version of the lemma can be found.

**Lemma.** *(continuous version of the Gronwall's lemma) Let $-\infty<a<b<+\infty$ and let $u:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be a Borel measurable integrable function. If there exist $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, $\beta\in [0,+\infty)$ such that for all $t\in [a,b]$ the function $u$ satisfies

$$
u(t)\leq \alpha+\beta\int\limits_a^t u(s)ds,
$$

then for all $t\in [a,b]$ we have that

$$
u(t)\leq \alpha e^{\beta(t-a)}.
$$

*

**Proof.** Let us define the function $h:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ as follows

$$
h(t)=\alpha+\beta\int\limits_a^t u(s)ds.
$$

Then, by the assumption

text:
$$
u(t)\leq h(t).
$$

for all $t\in [a,b]$. Moreover, $h$ is absolutely continuous and

$$
h'(t)=\beta\cdot u(t)
$$

for almost all $t$ in $[0,T]$. Since $\beta\geq 0$, we get from and that

$$
h'(t)\leq \beta h(t)
$$

for almost all $t$ in $[0,T]$. Furthermore, by

$$
\Bigl(e^{-\beta t}h(t)\Bigr)^{'}=-\beta e^{-\beta t}h(t)+e^{-\beta t}h'(t)\leq 0
$$

for almost all $t$ in $[0,T]$. The functions $[a,b]\ni t\to e^{-\beta t}$ and $h$ are absolutely continuous, hence so it is $[a,b]\ni t\to e^{-\beta t}h(t)$. Thereby

$$
e^{-\beta t}h(t)-e^{-\beta a}h(a)=\int\limits_a^t \Bigl(e^{-\beta s}h(s)\Bigr)^{'}ds\leq 0
$$

for all $t\in [a,b]$. Hence,

$$
u(t)\leq h(t)\leq e^{\beta (t-a)}h(a)=\alpha e^{\beta (t-a)}, \ t\in [a,b].
$$

This completes the proof.    $\blacksquare$\

Let $(X_i,\mathcal{A}_i)$, $i=1,2$, be measurable spaces. On the Cartesian product $X_1\times X_2$ of the sets $X_i$, $i=1,2$, we consider the so called *product* $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{A}_1\otimes \mathcal{A}_2$ defined by

$$
\mathcal{A}_1\otimes \mathcal{A}_2=\sigma\Bigl(\{A_1\times A_2 \ | \ A_i\in\mathcal{A}_i, i=1,2\}\Bigr).
$$

Then $(X_1\times X_2,\mathcal{A}_1\otimes \mathcal{A}_2)$ is a measurable space. Note that we also have

$$
\mathcal{A}_1\otimes \mathcal{A}_2=\sigma(\mathcal{\hat A}_1\cup \mathcal{\hat A}_2),
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{\hat A}_1=\{A\times X_2 \ | \ A\in\mathcal{A}_1\},\\
\mathcal{\hat A}_2=\{X_1\times B \ | \ B\in\mathcal{A}_2\},
$$

see page. 5 in . Now, let $(X_i,\mathcal{A}_i,\mu_i)$, $i=1,2$, be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces. Then there exists a unique measure $\mu_1\times \mu_2$ on the $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{A}_1\otimes \mathcal{A}_2$ such that

$$
(\mu_1\times \mu_2)(A_1\times A_2)=\mu_1(A_1)\cdot\mu_2(A_2)
$$

holds for any $A_i\in\mathcal{A}_i$, $i=1,2$. The measure $\mu_1\times \mu_2$ is called the *product measure*. Of course $(X_1\times X_2,\mathcal{A}_1\otimes \mathcal{A}_2,\mu_1\times \mu_2)$ is a measure space.

**Proposition.** *Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y_i,\mathcal{C}_i)$ be measurable spaces and let $f_i:X\to Y_i$ for $i=1,2$. Define $H:X\to Y_1\times Y_2$ by

$$
H(x)=(f_1,f_2)(x)=(f_1(x),f_2(x)), \ x\in X.
$$

Then $H$ is $\mathcal{A} / \mathcal{C}_1\otimes\mathcal{C}_2$-measurable iff $f_i:X\to Y_i$ is $\mathcal{A} / \mathcal{C}_i$-measurable for $i=1,2$.*

The proposition above has its multi-dimensional generalization, see, for example, Proposition, page 45 in or Lemma in .

Below we state the measurability of sections.
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
**Proposition.** *Let $(X_i,\mathcal{A}_i)$, $(Y,\mathcal{C})$, $i=1,2$, be measurable spaces. Let us assume $f:X_1\times X_2\to Y$ to be $\mathcal{A}_1\otimes\mathcal{A}_2 / \mathcal{C}$-measurable. For any $x\in X_1$ the section

$$
X_2\ni y\to f_x(y)=f(x,y)\in Y
$$

is $\mathcal{A}_2 /\mathcal{C}$-measurable, while for any $y\in X_2$ the section

$$
X_1\ni x\to f^y(x)=f(x,y)\in Y
$$

is $\mathcal{A}_1 /\mathcal{C}$-measurable.*

Hence, product measurability implies measurability of each section. We want to underline here that the converse is not true - without some additional requirements measurability of sections does not imply product measurability. We have however the following result, that is very useful from a point of view of stochastic processes (see, for example, page 46 in or Remark at page 5. in ).

**Lemma.** *Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let $f:X\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be such that the section $y\to f(x,y)$ is right-continuous (or left-continuous) for each $x\in X$ and that the section $x\to f(x,y)$ is $\mathcal{A} /\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable for each $y\in\mathbb{R}$. Then, $f$ is $\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable.*

Note that $f$ may be a mapping with values in a separable metric space (such as the euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^d$) and the thesis of Lemma still holds, see Lemma in .

**Theorem.** *(Tonelli's Theorem) Let $(X_i,\mathcal{A}_i,\mu_i)$, $i=1,2$, be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, and let $f:X_1\times X_2\to [0,+\infty]$ be $\mathcal{A}_1\otimes\mathcal{A}_2 / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{\bar R})$-measurable. Then*

- *the function

$$
X_1\ni x_1\to \int\limits_{X_2} f(x_1,x_2) \mu_2(dx_2)
$$

is $\mathcal{A}_1 /\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{\bar R})$-measurable and the function

$$
X_2\ni x_2\to \int\limits_{X_1} f(x_1,x_2) \mu_1(dx_1)
$$

is $\mathcal{A}_2 /\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{\bar R})$-measurable, and*

- *for the function $f$ the following holds

$$
\int\limits_{X_1\times X_2} f(x_1,x_2) \ \mu_1\times\mu_2(dx_1,dx_2)&=&\int\limits_{X_1}\Bigl(\int\limits_{X_2}f(x_1,x_2)\mu_2(dx_2)\Bigr)\mu_1(dx_1)\\
&=&\int\limits_{X_2}\Bigl(\int\limits_{X_1}f(x_1,x_2)\mu_1(dx_1)\Bigr)\mu_2(dx_2).
$$

*
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
We stress that we can use for every nonnegative and $\mathcal{A}_1\otimes\mathcal{A}_2 / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{\bar R})$-measurable function $f$, no matter if it is $\mu_1\times \mu_2$-integrable or not. Hence, for an arbitrary $\mathcal{A}_1\otimes\mathcal{A}_2 / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{\bar R})$-measurable function $f:X_1\times X_2\to \mathbb{\bar R}$ we can check if it is $\mu_1\times \mu_2$-integrable by applying to $\displaystyle{\int\limits_{X_1\times X_2} |f(x_1,x_2)| \ \mu_1\times\mu_2(dx_1,dx_2)}$. Such situation occurs many times in the theory of stochastic processes.

**Theorem.** *(Fubini's Theorem) Let $(X_i,\mathcal{A}_i,\mu_i)$, $i=1,2$, be $\sigma$-finite measure spaces, and let $f:X_1\times X_2\to [-\infty,+\infty]$ be $\mathcal{A}_1\otimes\mathcal{A}_2 / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{\bar R})$-measurable and $\mu_1\times\mu_2$-integrable. Then*

- *for $\mu_1$-almost every $x_1\in X_1$ the section $f_{x_1}$ is $\mu_2$-integrable and for $\mu_2$-almost every $x_2\in X_2$ the section $f^{x_2}$ is $\mu_1$-integrable,*

- *the functions $I_f$ and $J_f$ defined by

$$
I_f(x_1)=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\int\limits_{X_2}f_{x_1}(x_2)\mu_2(dx_2) & \ \hbox{if} \ f_{x_1} \ \hbox{is} \ \mu_2-\hbox{integrable} , \\
0 & \ \hbox{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.
$$

and

$$
J_f(x_2)=\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\int\limits_{X_1}f^{x_2}(x_1)\mu_1(dx_1) & \ \hbox{if} \ f^{x_2} \ \hbox{is} \ \mu_1-\hbox{integrable} , \\
0 & \ \hbox{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.
$$

belong to $L^1(X_1,\mathcal{A}_1,\mu_1;\mathbb{R})$ and $L^1(X_2,\mathcal{A}_2,\mu_2;\mathbb{R})$, respectively, and*

- *the relation

$$
\int\limits_{X_1\times X_2} f(x_1,x_2) \ \mu_1\times\mu_2(dx_1,dx_2)=\int\limits_{X_1}I_f(x_1)\mu_1(dx_1)=\int\limits_{X_2}J_f(x_2)\mu_2(dx_2)
$$

holds.*

Proofs of Theorems and (and their generalizations to a product of finite number of $\sigma$-finite measure spaces) can be found in .

Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space, i.e., a measure space such that $\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1$. A $\Sigma / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$-measurable function $\xi:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is called a random variable (or a random vector). If $(X,\mathcal{A})$ is a measurable space then we call a function $\xi:\Omega\to X$ a ($X$-valued) *random element* (or a *random function*) provided that it is $\Sigma / \mathcal{A}$-measurable. The law of $\xi$ is given by

$$
\mu(A)=\mathbb{P}(\{\xi \in A\})=\mathbb{P}(\xi^{-1}(A)),
$$
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
for all $A\in\mathcal{A}$. Hence, the random element $\xi$ induces measure on $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and then the space $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$ is a measure space equipped with the probability measure $\mu$ ($\mu(X)=1$). The classical example is a Wiener space $(C([0,T]),\mathcal{B}(C([0,T])), w)$ equipped with the Wiener measure $w$. The measure $w$ is a law of the random element $\hat W:\Omega\to C([0,T])$, generated by a Wiener process $W$ (see Theorem ).

Below we recall the Central Limit Theorem. For the proof see, for example, Theorem in .

**Theorem.** *(Central Limit Theorem, CLT) Let $(X_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ be an i.i.d sequence of random variables with common mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Let $\displaystyle{S_n=\sum\limits_{j=1}^n X_j, n\in\mathbb{N}}$. Then the sequence

$$
\Bigl(\frac{S_n-\mathbb{E}(S_n)}{\sqrt{Var(S_n)}}\Bigr)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
$$

converges in distribution to a normal distribution with mean $0$ and variance $1$.*

Note that under the assumptions of Theorem

$$
\frac{S_n-\mathbb{E}(S_n)}{\sqrt{Var(S_n)}}=\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}=\sqrt{n}\frac{\bar S_n-\mu}{\sigma},
$$

where $\displaystyle{\bar S_n=S_n/n}$.

The following result is a vary useful consequence of Borel-Cantelli lemma.

**Theorem.** *() Let $\alpha>0$ and $K(p)\in [0,+\infty)$ for $p\geq 1$. In addition, let $Z_n$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, be a sequence of random variables such that

$$
\Bigl(\mathbb{E}|Z_n|^p\Bigr)^{1/p}\leq K(p)\cdot n^{-\alpha}
$$

for all $p\geq 1$ and all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then for all $\varepsilon\in (0,\alpha)$ there exists a random variable $\eta_{\varepsilon}$ such that

$$
|Z_n|\leq \eta_{\varepsilon}\cdot n^{-\alpha+\varepsilon} \ \hbox{almost surely}
$$

for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Moreover, $\mathbb{E}|\eta_{\varepsilon}|^p<+\infty$ for all $p\geq 1$.*

Below we recall the famous Burkholder inequality, which is nowadays widely used when establishing error bounds for Monte Carlo algorithms (for references, see, , ). For the exposition of the inequality we need a notion of a filtration and martingale in the discrete-time case.
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
A *discrete filtration* on a probability space $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ is an increasing family $(\Sigma_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ of sub-$\sigma$-fields of $\Sigma$. A sequence $M=(M_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued random variables on $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ is said to be a *discrete-time martingale* with respect to $(\Sigma_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ provided that

- $M=(M_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is adapted to $(\Sigma_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$, i.e., $\sigma(M_n)\subset\Sigma_n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$,

- $\mathbb{E}\|M_n\|_2<+\infty$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$,

- $\mathbb{E}(M_{n+1} \ | \ \Sigma_n)=M_n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$.

We now recall two main inequalities for discrete-time martingales.

**Theorem.** *(Hoeffding inequality - orginal version, ) Let $(X_i)_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}$ be a sequence of independent random variables such that $a_i\leq X_i\leq b_i$ with probability one for $i=1,2,\ldots,n$ and for some real numbers $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, $b_1,\ldots,b_n$. Let $\displaystyle{S_n=\sum\limits_{k=1}^n X_k}$. Then for all $t>0$

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(|S_n-\mathbb{E}(S_n)|>t\Bigr)\leq 2\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (b_i-a_i)^2}\Bigr).
$$

*

**Theorem.** *(Hoeffding-Azuma inequality, ) Let $(M_j)_{j=0,1,\ldots,n}$ be a real-valued martingale such that $|M_j-M_{j-1}|\leq a_j$ a.s. for all $j=1,2,\ldots,n$. Then, for all $r\geq 0$

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(|M_n-M_0|\geq r\Bigr)\leq 2 \exp\Biggl(-\frac{r^2}{2\sum\limits_{j=1}^na_j^2}\Biggr).
$$

*

**Theorem.** *(Burkholder's inequality, ) For each $p\in (1,+\infty)$ there exist positive constants $c_p$ and $C_p$ such that for every $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued discrete-time martingale $M=(M_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ and for every $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$ we have

$$
c_p\|[M]_n^{1/2}\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\leq \Bigl\|\max\limits_{0\leq j \leq n} \|M_j\|_2 \Bigl\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\leq C_p\|[M]_n^{1/2}\|_{L^p(\Omega)},
$$

where $\displaystyle{[M]_n=\|M_0\|^2_2+\sum\limits_{k=1}^n \|M_k-M_{k-1}\|^2_2}$ is the quadratic variation of $M$.*

In the case when $p\in [2,+\infty)$ we show some useful upper estimates for $\|[M]_n^{1/2}\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$. Firstly, let us denote by $\Delta M_k:=M_k-M_{k-1}$ for $k=,1,2,\ldots,n$ and $\Delta M_0:=M_0$. Then, by the triangle inequality
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
$$\|[M]_n^{1/2}\|^2_{L^p(\Omega)}=\|[M]_n\|_{L^{p/2}(\Omega)}=\Bigl\|\sum_{k=0}^n\|\Delta M_k\|_2^2\Bigl\|_{L^{p/2}(\Omega)}\leq \sum_{k=0}^n\Bigl\|\|\Delta M_k\|_2^2\Bigl\|_{L^{p/2}(\Omega)}=\sum_{k=0}^n \|\Delta M_k\|^2_{L^p(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^d)},$$

hence

$$
\Bigl\|\max\limits_{0\leq j \leq n} \|M_j\|_2 \Bigl\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\leq C_p\Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^n \|\Delta M_k\|^2_{L^p(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^d)}\Bigr)^{1/2}.
$$

Next, by the Hölder inequality

$$
\sum_{k=0}^n\|\Delta M_k\|^2_{L^p(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^d)}\leq \Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^n \|\Delta M_k\|^p_{L^p(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^d)}\Bigr)^{2/p}\cdot (n+1)^{1-\frac{2}{p}}.
$$

Combining the estimates above we obtain

$$
\Bigl\|\max\limits_{0\leq j \leq n} \|M_j\|_2 \Bigl\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\leq C_p\Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^n \|\Delta M_k\|^2_{L^p(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^d)}\Bigr)^{1/2}\leq C_p\cdot (n+1)^{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{p}}\cdot\Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^n \|\Delta M_k\|^p_{L^p(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^d)}\Bigr)^{1/p}.
$$

We also recall definition of a martingale and a local martingale in continuous time.

An $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued stochastic process $M=(M(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ on $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ is said to be a *continuous-time martingale* with respect to the given filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ provided that

- $M=(M(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is adapted to $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$, i.e., $\sigma(M(t))\subset\Sigma_t$ for all $t\in [0,+\infty)$,

- $\mathbb{E}\|M(t)\|_2<+\infty$ for all $t\in [0,+\infty)$,

- $\mathbb{E}(M(t) \ | \ \Sigma_s)=M(s)$ for all $0\leq s<t$.

A random variable $\tau:\Omega\to [0,+\infty]$ is said to be *stopping time* with respect to the filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ if, for every $t\in [0,+\infty)$,

$$
\{\tau\leq t\}\in\Sigma_t.
$$

We also set

$$
\Sigma_{\tau}=\{A\in\Sigma \ | \ \forall_{t\in [0,+\infty)} \ A\cap\{\tau\leq t\}\in\Sigma_t\}.
$$

An $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued stochastic process $M=(M(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ on $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ is said to be a *continuous-time local martingale* with respect to the given filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ if it is adapted to $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ and if there exists an increasing sequence $(\tau_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$-stopping times such that

- $\mathbb{P}(\lim\limits_{n\to +\infty}\tau_n=+\infty)=1$,

- for every $n$ the process $(M(t\wedge\tau_n),\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is a martingale.

Let $\{\mathcal{F}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{F}_m\}$ be a family of sub-$\sigma$-fields of $\Sigma$. W call this collection *a family of independent $\sigma$-fields* or we say that the $\sigma$-fields $\mathcal{F}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{F}_m$ are *(mutually) independent* if, for every $A_1\in\mathcal{F}_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathcal{F}_m$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A_1\cap\ldots \cap A_m)=\mathbb{P}(A_1)\cdot\ldots\cdot\mathbb{P}(A_m).
$$

Independence of events from $\Sigma$ can also be expressed in the term of independent $\sigma$-fields. Namely, the events $A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\Sigma$ are independent iff the $\sigma$-fields $\sigma(\{A_1\}),\ldots,\sigma(\{A_m\})$ are independent, where $\sigma(\{A_i\})=\{\emptyset,\Omega,A_i,\Omega\setminus A_i\}$.

Random elements $\xi_j:\Omega\to X_j$, with values in arbitrary measurable spaces $(X_j,\mathcal{A}_j)$, $j=1,2,\ldots,m$, are *independent* if and only if the $\sigma$-fields $\sigma(\xi_1),\ldots,\sigma(\xi_m)$ are independent. Note that the independence of the events $A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\Sigma$ is equivalent to the independence of the random variables $\mathbf{1}_{A_1},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{A_m}$.

For a (possibly infinite) family $(\xi_i)_{i\in I}$ of random elements we say that they are *independent* if and only if the random elements $\xi_{i_1},\ldots,\xi_{i_m}$ are independent for every choice of a finite number $i_1,\ldots,i_m$ of distinct indices in $I$. An analogous definition holds for an infinite family $(\mathcal{F}_i)_{i\in I}$ of sub-$\sigma$-fields of $\Sigma$.

Let $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of (arbitrary) subsets of $\Sigma$. We say that $\mathcal{A}_i$'s are *(mutually) independent* iff for any finite subset $J$ of $I$ and for any $A_j\in\mathcal{A}_{j}$, $j\in J$, it holds

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j\Bigr)=\prod\limits_{j\in J}\mathbb{P}(A_j).
$$

**Lemma.** *Let $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of $\pi$-systems and $\mathcal{A}_i\subset\Sigma$ for $i\in I$. Then $(\sigma(\mathcal{A}_i))_{i\in I}$ is a family of independent $\sigma$-fields iff $(\mathcal{A}_i)_{i\in I}$ are independent.*

W also say that the random element $\xi$ is independent of the sub-$\sigma$-field $\mathcal{G}\subset\Sigma$ if the $\sigma$-fields $\sigma(\xi)$ and $\mathcal{G}$ are independent.

The following simple but useful lemma holds.
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
**Lemma.** *Let $\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_m$, $\mathcal{B}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{B}_m$, $\mathcal{C}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{C}_m$ be a sub-$\sigma$-fields of $\Sigma$. Moreover, we assume that*

- *$\mathcal{A}_i,\mathcal{B}_i\subset\mathcal{C}_i$ for all $i=1,\ldots,m$,*

- *$(\mathcal{C}_i)_{i=1,\ldots,m}$ is a family of independent $\sigma$-fields,*

- *for all $i=1,\ldots,m$ the $\sigma$-fields $\mathcal{A}_i$ and $\mathcal{B}_i$ are independent.*

*Then $\{\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_m,\mathcal{B}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{B}_m\}$ is a family of independent $\sigma$-fields.*

**Proof.** Let us take arbitrary $A_i\in\mathcal{A}_i$, $B_i\in\mathcal{B}_i$, $i=1,\ldots,m$. By the assumption (i) we have $A_i\cap B_i\in\mathcal{C}_i$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$, and by the assumptions (ii), (iii) we get

$$
&&\mathbb{P}(A_1\cap\ldots\cap A_m\cap B_1\cap\ldots\cap B_m)=\mathbb{P}((A_1\cap B_1)\cap\ldots\cap(A_m\cap B_m))\\
&&=\prod\limits_{j=1}^m\mathbb{P}(A_j\cap B_j)=\prod\limits_{j=1}^m\mathbb{P}(A_j)\mathbb{P}(B_j).
$$

This ends the proof.    $\blacksquare$\
\
Pairwise independence is much weaker than being mutually independent. However, independence can be checked by repeated checks for pairwise independence, see, for example, or .

**Proposition.** *The sub-$\sigma$-fields $\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2,\ldots$ of $\Sigma$ are independent if and only if $\bigvee_{i=1,\ldots,n}\mathcal{F}_i$ and $\mathcal{F}_{n+1}$ are independent for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.*

We also recall the grouping property, see, for example, .

**Proposition.** *Let $(\mathcal{F})_{i\in I}$ be a family of independent sub-$\sigma$-fields of $\Sigma$, and let $\mathcal{T}$ be a disjoint partition of $I$. Then the $\sigma$-fields

$$
\mathcal{F}_{S}=\bigvee_{s\in S}\mathcal{F}_s, \ S\in\mathcal{T},
$$

are again independent.*

Independence has its consequence for the product of random variables.

**Lemma.** *Let $X,Y$ be independent and integrable random variables. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}(X\cdot Y)=\mathbb{E}(X)\cdot\mathbb{E}(Y).
$$

The same holds true if $X,Y$ are nonnegative and not necessarily integrable.*

The proof of the following projection property of conditional expectation can be found, for example, in .

**Theorem.** *Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\Sigma$. For every $X\in L^2(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ we have
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
$$
\mathbb{E}\Bigl(X-\mathbb{E}( X \ | \ \mathcal{G})\Bigr)^2=\inf\limits_{Y\in L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{G},\mathbb{P})}\mathbb{E}(X-Y)^2.
$$

*

**Theorem.** *(Conditional Fubini's Theorem, ) Suppose that $X\in L^1(\Omega\times [0,T],\Sigma\otimes \mathcal{B}([0,T]),\mathbb{P}\times\lambda_1)$ and let $\mathcal{G}$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\Sigma$. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}\Bigl(\int\limits_0^T X(t)dt \ | \ \mathcal{G}\Bigr)=\int\limits_0^T \mathbb{E}(X(t) \ | \ \mathcal{G}) \ dt \ a.s.
$$

*

**Theorem.** *(The freezing lemma, ) Let $X$ and $Y$ be respectively a $d$-dimensional and a $k$-dimensional random vector, and let $\psi:\mathbb{R}^{d+k}\to\mathbb{R}$ be Borel measurable such that $\psi(X,Y)\geq 0$ a.s., or $\mathbb{E}|\psi(X,Y)|<+\infty$. Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\Sigma$ such that $X$ is $\mathcal{G}$-measurable, and $\sigma(Y)$, $\mathcal{G}$ are independent $\sigma$-fields. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}\Bigl(\psi(X,Y) \ | \ \mathcal{G}\Bigr)=\mathbb{E}\Bigl(\psi(x, Y)\Bigr)\Bigl|_{x=X}=\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^k}\psi(X,y)\mathbb{P}_Y(dy).
$$

*

The following fact can be found for example in , page 238.

**Lemma.** *Let $W=(W(t))_{t\in [0,T]}$ be the Wiener process with respect to the filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,T]}$. If $f\in L^2([0,T])$ is a deterministic function, then for all $t\in [0,T]$ the $\sigma$-fields $\displaystyle{\sigma\Bigl(\int\limits_t^T f(s)dW(s)\Bigr)}$ and $\Sigma_t$ are independent.*
title: Foundations of Monte Carlo Methods and Stochastic Simulations (lecture notes, arXiv)

text:
In this section we recall basic facts from the theory of continuous-time stochastic processes.

Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ be a *complete probability space*, that is all subsets of measure zero sets are also measurable (and hence, also of measure zero). We consider the product space $(\Omega\times [0,+\infty),\Sigma\otimes \mathcal{B}([0,+\infty)),\mathbb{P}\times \lambda_1)$. By a stochastic process $X$, with the base probability space $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ and with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we mean a mapping

$$
X:\Omega\times [0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^d,
$$

such that for each $t\in [0,+\infty)$ the function

$$
\Omega\ni \omega\to X(t,\omega)\in\mathbb{R}^d
$$

is $\Sigma / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$-measurable, i.e., it is a random variable. We usually use the following notational convention $X=(X(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$, which, in particular, underlines that a stochastic process might be seen as a collection of random variables. For a fixed $\omega\in\Omega$ the $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued function

$$
[0,+\infty)\ni t\to X(\omega,t)\in\mathbb{R}^d
$$

is called a *trajectory* (or *realization* or *sample function*) corresponding to the elementary event $\omega$. Note that, without any additional assumptions imposed on $X$, such a trajectory might not be even measurable. We say that the stochastic process $X$ is *product measurable* if it is $\Sigma\otimes \mathcal{B}([0,+\infty)) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ - measurable. The following widely used fact is a direct consequence of a product measurability and Fubini's theorem.

**Proposition.** *Let $X=(X(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ be a product measurable stochastic process. Then*

- *All trajectories of $X$ are $\mathcal{B}([0,+\infty) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$-measurable functions.*

- *For any $t\in [0,+\infty)$ the function

$$
\Omega\ni\omega\to X(\omega,t)\in \mathbb{R}^d
$$

is $\Sigma / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$-measurable, so it is $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued random variable.*

- *if $\mathbb{E}(X(t))$ exists for all $t\in [0,+\infty)$ then

$$
[0,+\infty)\ni t\to\mathbb{E}(X(t))\in \mathbb{R}^d
$$

is $\mathcal{B}([0,+\infty)) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$-measurable.*

- *if $A\in\mathcal{B}([0,+\infty))$ and $\displaystyle{\int\limits_{A}\mathbb{E}|X(t)|dt<+\infty}$, then

$$
\int\limits_A|X(t)|dt<+\infty \ \hbox{almost surely},
$$

and

$$
\int\limits_A \mathbb{E}(X(t))dt=\mathbb{E}\Bigl(\int\limits_A X(t) dt\Bigr).
$$

text:
Let $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ be a family of sub-$\sigma$-fields of $\Sigma$, such that

$$
\Sigma_s\subset\Sigma_t\subset\Sigma, \ \hbox{for all} \ 0\leq s<t.
$$

Then we call $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ the *filtration* on $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$. Moreover, we set

$$
\Sigma_{\infty}=\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{t\geq 0}\Sigma_t\Bigr).
$$

Of course $\Sigma_{\infty}\subset\Sigma$. We say that the filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is *complete* if

$$
\mathcal{N}\subset\Sigma_0,
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{N}=\{A\in\Sigma \ | \ \mathbb{P}(A)=0\}.
$$

If $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is not complete then we can always take

$$
\bar\Sigma_t=\sigma(\Sigma_t\cup\mathcal{N}), \ t\in [0,+\infty).
$$

Of course the filtration $(\bar\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is complete and it is called *augmented* filtration. The filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is called *right-continuous* if $\Sigma_t=\Sigma_{t+}$ for all $t\in [0,+\infty)$, where $\displaystyle{\Sigma_{t+}=\bigcap_{s>t}\Sigma_s}$. (We have that $\Sigma_t\subset\Sigma_{t+}$ for all $t\in [0,+\infty)$ and the family $(\Sigma_{t+})_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is already a right-continuous filtration.) If $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is complete and right-continuous then we say that it satisfies the *usual conditions*. Note that the filtration $(\tilde\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$, where

$$
\tilde\Sigma_t=\bigcap_{s>t}\bar\Sigma_s \ (=\bar\Sigma_{t+}),
$$

always satisfies the usual conditions, even if the initial filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ does not.

If for all $t\in [0,+\infty)$

$$
\sigma(X(t))\subset \Sigma_t,
$$

then we say that the stochastic process $X=(X(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is adapted to $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$. Every stochastic process $X$ is adapted to $(\Sigma^X_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ where

$$
\Sigma_t^X=\sigma(X(s) \ | \ s\in [0,t])=\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{s\in [0,t]} \sigma(X(s))\Bigr).
$$

We call $(\Sigma^X_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ the *natural filtration* of the process $X$. This is the smallest filtration to which $X$ is adapted. We stress that the natural filtration of $X$ neither have to be complete nor right-continuous, while $(\tilde\Sigma^X_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ satisfies the usual conditions. Analogously we also define the last element of $(\Sigma_t^X)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ by

$$
\Sigma_{\infty}^X=\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{t\geq 0}\Sigma_t^X\Bigr).
$$

text:
**Definition.** Suppose that $X=(X(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ and $Y=(Y(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$, are two $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued stochastic processes defined on the same probability space $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$.

- We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **stochastically equivalent** if

$$
\forall_{t\in [0,+\infty)} \ \mathbb{P}\Bigl(\{\omega\in\Omega \ |\ X(\omega,t)=Y(\omega,t)\}\Bigr)=1.
$$

We then say that $Y$ is a **modification** (or a **version**) of $X$.

- We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **indistinguishable** if

$$
\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\{\omega\in\Omega \ | \ \forall_{t\in [0,+\infty)} \ X(\omega,t)=Y(\omega,t)\}\Bigr)=1.
$$

Of course if two processes are indistinguishable then they are stochastically equivalent, but the converse is in general not true. However, the following important result holds, see .

**Theorem.** *Suppose that $X=(X(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ and $Y=(Y(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ are stochastically equivalent, and that both processes are almost surely right-(or left-) continuous. Then they are indistinguishable.*

In summary, we have four different ways in which we can say that two stochastic processes are equal:

- $X(\omega,t)=Y(\omega,t)$ for all $(\omega,t)\in \Omega\times [0,+\infty)$, but this situation occurs rarely,

- $X$ and $Y$ are stochastically equivalent,

- $X$ and $Y$ are indistinguishable,

- $X=Y$ $d\mathbb{P}\times d\lambda_1$-almost everywhere, i.e.,

$$
(\mathbb{P}\times\lambda_1)\Bigl(\{(\omega,t)\in\Omega\times [0,+\infty) \ | \ X(\omega,t)\neq Y(\omega,t)\}\Bigr)=0.
$$

In order to use that notion of equivalence we have to assume that $X$ and $Y$ are product measurable processes.

section: What does it mean that two processes are equivalent?

text:
Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P})$ be a complete probability space with a filtration $(\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ satisfying the usual conditions. We consider the following classes of stochastic processes

$$
\mathbb{D}=\{X:\Omega\times [0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^d \ | \ X \ \hbox{is adapted to} \ (\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)} \ \hbox{and has c\`adl\`ag paths}\},
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{L}=\{X:\Omega\times [0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^d \ | \ X \ \hbox{is adapted to} \ (\Sigma_t)_{t\in [0,+\infty)} \ \hbox{and has c\`agl\`ad paths}\}.
$$

Then, the *predictable $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{P}$* on $\Omega\times [0,+\infty)$ is the smallest $\sigma$-field making all processes in $\mathbb{L}$ measurable, i.e.,

$$
\mathcal{P}=\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup\limits_{X\in \mathbb{L}}\sigma(X)\Bigr).
$$

The *optional $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{O}$* on $\Omega\times [0,+\infty)$ is the smallest $\sigma$-field making all processes in $\mathbb{D}$ measurable, i.e.,

$$
\mathcal{O}=\sigma\Bigl(\bigcup\limits_{X\in \mathbb{D}}\sigma(X)\Bigr).
$$

A stochastic process $X=(X(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is called *progressive* or *progressively measurable* if for each $t\in [0,+\infty)$ the mapping

$$
\Omega\times [0,t] \ni (\omega,s)\to X(\omega,s)\in\mathbb{R}^d
$$

is $\Sigma_t\otimes\mathcal{B}([0,t]) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d)$-measurable. The *progressive $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{A}$* on $\Omega\times [0,+\infty)$ is the smallest $\sigma$-field that makes all progressive processes measurable. We have that

$$
\mathcal{P}\subset\mathcal{O}\subset\mathcal{A}\subset \Sigma\otimes\mathcal{B}([0,+\infty)),
$$

see . For the proof of the fact below we refer to .

**Proposition.** *Let $f:[0,+\infty)\to \mathbb{R}^d$ be a Borel function and let us consider the (deterministic process) $X(\omega,t)=f(t)$ for all $(\omega,t)\in \Omega\times [0,+\infty)$. Then $X=(X(t))_{t\in [0,+\infty)}$ is predictable.*

section: Three notions of measurability of stochastic processes

text:
Sometimes it is convenient to switch between two possible ways of looking at stochastic processes. The first possibility is to consider a stochastic process $X$ as a product measurable function with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$. However, if (almost) all trajectories of $X$ belong to some functional space $E$ equipped with $\sigma$-field $\mathcal{E}$, then we can consider a mapping $\hat X:\Omega\to E$ defined as

$$
\hat X(\omega)=X(\omega,\cdot), \ \omega\in\Omega.
$$

If $\hat X$ is $\Sigma / \mathcal{E}$-measurable then we say that the process $X$ generates the random element $\hat X$ in $(E,\mathcal{E})$. Moreover, the law $\mu$ of $\hat X$ is a probabilistic measure induced by $\hat X$ on the measure space $(E,\mathcal{E})$, see .

We listed below three most common cases. For the proofs see, for example, .

**Theorem.**

- *Let $E=C([0,T])$, equipped with supremum norm $\|\cdot\|_{\infty}$, and $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{B}(E)$. If $X$ is a stochastic process with continuous trajectories, then it generates a random element in $C([0,T])$.*

- *Let $E=D([0,T])$ be the Skorokhod space, equipped with the Skorokhod metric $d$, and $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{B}(E)$. If $X$ is a stochastic process with càdlàg trajectories, then it generates a random element in $D([0,T])$.*

- *Let $E=L^2([0,T])$, equipped with the norm $\|\cdot\|_{L^2([0,T])}$, and $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{B}(E)$. If $X\in L^2(\Omega\times [0,T],\Sigma\otimes\mathcal{B}([0,T]),\mathbb{P}\times\lambda_1)$, then it generates a random element in $L^2([0,T])$.*

Having a random element $\hat X$ in some functional space $E$ it is natural to ask if there is a product measurable stochastic process $X$ satisfying . In the case when $E=L^2([0,T])$ the situation is more subtle since $L^2([0,T])$ consists of equivalence classes.

**Theorem.**

*Let $\hat X$ be a random element in $C([0,T])$. Then the process $X$ defined by

$$
X(\omega,t)=(\hat X(\omega))(t), (\omega,t)\in \Omega\times [0,T],
$$

is product measurable and has continuous trajectories.*

*Let $\hat X$ be a random element in $D([0,T])$. Then the process $X$ defined by is product measurable and has càdlàg trajectories.*

*Let $\hat X$ be a random element in $L^2([0,T])$. Then there exists a product measurable process $X$ such that for almost all $\omega$, the equality $\displaystyle{X(\omega,t)=(\hat X(\omega))(t)}$ holds almost everywhere on $[0,T]$.*

section: Stochastic process as a random element with values in functional space and vice versa

text:
For the proof of $(iii)$ see Proposition 2, page 741. in . In order to show $(i)$ and $(ii)$ we recall after what follows.

**Lemma.**

- *The coordinate mappings $\delta_t:C([0,T])\to \mathbb{R}$ defined by

$$
\delta_t (f)=f(t), \ f\in C([0,T])
$$

are $\mathcal{B}(C([0,T])) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable for all $t\in [0,T]$.*

- *The coordinate mappings $\delta_t:D([0,T])\to \mathbb{R}$ defined by

$$
\delta_t (f)=f(t), \ f\in D([0,T])
$$

are $\mathcal{B}(D([0,T])) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable for all $t\in [0,T]$.*

**Proof of Theorem (i).** For any $t\in [0,T]$ we can write as

$$
X(\omega,t)=\delta_t(\hat X(\omega)), \omega\in\Omega.
$$

By Lemma (a) and from the fact that the random element $\hat X$ is $\Sigma /\mathcal{B}(C([0,T]))$-measurable, we get for any $B\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ that

$$
(X(t))^{-1}(B)=\Bigl(\delta_t(\hat X)\Bigr)^{-1}(B)=\hat X^{-1}(\delta_t^{-1}(B)) \in\Sigma,
$$

so for any $t\in [0,T]$ the mapping

$$
\Omega\ni\omega\to X(\omega,t)\in\mathbb{R}
$$

is $\Sigma / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable. For any $\omega\in\Omega$ we have that $\hat X(\omega)\in C([0,T])$. Hence, by we get that for any $\omega\in\Omega$ the function

$$
[0,T]\ni t\to X(\omega,t)\in\mathbb{R}
$$

is continuous. By Lemma we obtain that $X$ is $\Sigma\otimes \mathcal{B}([0,T]) / \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable.    $\blacksquare$\
\
The proof of Theorem (ii) is analogous and therefore it is left as an exercise.

**Remark.** *The spaces $C([0,T])$, $L^2([0,T])$ considered in Theorem (i), (iii) are separable Banach spaces. Hence, the random elements in Theorem (i), (iii) are Bochner measurable. Since the space $D([0,T])$, under the Skorokhod metric $d$, is complete separable metric space, the random element in Theorem (ii) is Borel measurable. (Recall also that the vector space $D([0,T])$ under the supremum norm is Banach but not separable.)*

Investors, who buy options in order to hedge a risk, use them in the same way as
an insurance police. For example, consider an European investor who is planning
to buy a factory in the USA which costs 10 million USD. The amount of money
is payable in three months. If the investor is worried about a devaluation of the
currency rate of the Euro he may consider to buy an options which gives him the
right to buy 10 million USD for a fixed exchange rate in three month. Thus, the
exercise price can be interpreted as a worst-case scenario. On the other hand, investors may also buy options to speculate on price movements of the underlying assets. If the price of the underlying climbs by onepercent the value of a corresponding European call usually climbs by a much larger
amount. Therefore, the investor makes a larger profit by investing the same amount
of money in the option instead of directly buying the underlying asset. Of course,
the same holds true for possible losses if the price of the underlying asset moves
in the wrongdirection. 1.2 Asset Price Model

assumed to be constant. By B(t) we denote the balance of the bank account. In practice, Assumption 1.2 is not satisfied for several reasons: The interest
rate is usually not fixed and banks often charge a higher interest rate on credits
than they pay on saving accounts. However, we interpret our assumption as an
approximation of the reality on short time intervals. If we put an amount of B0 on the account at time t0 then, at time t1 > t0, we

vanished. Therefore, in practice, if arbitrage opportunities exist in an efficient and

1.4 Monte Carlo Methods for Financial Option Valuation
The Black-Scholes formula (1.10) gives an analytic solution to the problem of
determining the fair value of a European call option. Therefore, we could consider
the problem as beingsolved. However, as it is pointed out by D. Higham [13, 14],
there are many variations of the option valuation problem, where a simpleanalytic
solution does not exist. For instance, this is true for so called exotic options [14], where the payoff not
only depends on the final time asset price, but also on its behaviour during the
time interval [0,T ]. The same problem occurs when we invoke a different asset
price model. For example, we refer to [22, Ch. 9.2] for several variations. The aim of this section and, in fact, of the whole lecture is to present and analyze numerical methods for applications where analytic solutions are not available. Here, we focus on Monte Carlo methods. Roughly speaking, a Monte Carlo
method tries to approximate the mean of a randomvariable X by the average over
a largenumber N of independent outcomes of X, that is N∑

Generating Random Numbers
In this section we describe different approaches to generate random numbers. In
particular, we discuss some algorithms which produce pseudo-random numbers. The goodness of these algorithms is analysed through a set of statistical tests. At
the end of this section we have a look at the Mersenne Twister, which is a widely
used pseudo-randomnumber generator. 3.1 Motivation
As it was pointed out in the introduction there exists a growing interest in modelling real world phenomenas which appear to be random. But before we can use a
computer to get any insights from one of these models we are facing the veryelementary problem that we work with a completely deterministic machine to model
random behaviour. So we are in need of some source of randomness. The first approaches to overcome this problem were built-in physical devices
in computers which generated random numbers by atomic decay or cosmic ray
counters. Another possibility are large databases of random numbers which were
generated by real random phenomena. But in practice, these solutions have several shortcomings. For example, in
modern applications in finance it is important to recompute the value of stock
options very fast after a significant change of one of the model parameters. Thus,
it is too slow if our physical device gives only one randomnumber every ten seconds or tooexpensive to buy a million of these devices to get sufficiently many
random numbers in the desired time horizon.
title: Numerical Methods for Stochastic Processes (Bielefeld lecture notes)

text:
In that regard databases are better suited. But here we have the problem that
such a database may be too small or may take too much memory. A database
with one billion random numbers takes already one gigabyte of memory if every
randomnumber takes exactly one byte. 34 3 Generating Random Numbers
 Another issue is that one can think of several physical or chemical processes
that could be used to generate random numbers. But they are onlyuseful for statistical purposes if oneexactly knows their distribution, which may varyover time. In this section we mainlyconsider another approach, the so called pseudorandom number generator (PRNG). These algorithms produce numbers U1,U2,... which are completely deterministic but mimic a certain random behaviour. In particular, we will focus on generators whose outputs look like an independent and
identically distributed sequence of U(0,1) random numbers. In today’s practice,
PRN Gs are most often used in statistical applications. Which random source one should choose in practice depends on the importance
of the following criteria in the given application: • Statistical properties,
• Speed and efficiency,
• Number of available random numbers,
• Reproducibility. In any case one should always be careful about using results which are derived with the help of randomnumber generators. As N. Madras points out in
[21, Ch. 2.3] it is onlyrecommended to use randomnumber generators which
have been tested thoroughly. In critical applications, it is worth to run simulations
twiceusing different randomnumber generators. One may think of many more sources of randomness which are not mentioned
here. As a starting point to this veryactive research field we refer to the discussion
in [10, Ch. 1]. Let us finally mention that, despite considerable progress in actual
computations, the question of a proper notion of a randomsequence remains one
of the fundamental problems in Mathematics, see the enlightening discussion in
[16, Ch.3]. 3.2 Pseudo-RandomNumber Generators
In this paragraph we loosely follow [9, Ch. 3.2.2] and [21, Ch. 2.2]. We give a definition of the class of generators which produce independent U(0,1)-distributed
pseudo-random numbers and introduce some terminology. We conclude with three
examples. Since computers can only store values of finite accuracy it is natural to consider
generators which produce random integers in a finite set {0,1,...,M − 1}.
